chunks: "A reflection is part of a signal bouncing back when it hits a change in impedance. A wave travelling on a transmission line sees the line's characteristic impedance.

If it reaches something with a different impedance, like the end of the line, a connector or a stub, the voltage and current on both sides of the junction have to match up, and the only way to do that is to send some of the wave back.
The fraction that comes back is equals (Z L-Z 0) over (Z L plus Z 0) . Open end: equals plus 1 , the whole wave comes back with the same sign and the voltage doubles.
Short: -1 , it comes back inverted. Load equal to Z 0 : zero, everything is absorbed. I care because the reflection travels back, and if the driver isn't matched it bounces again.
You get ringing and overshoot on every edge. For example, a 3. 3 volts driver with a 10 ohm output impedance into an unterminated 50 ohm trace launches about 2.
75 volts and the open end doubles it to 5. 5 volts, well past the supply rail and enough to hit the input clamp diodes.
It can also cause false clock edges when the ring crosses a threshold, delay the edge through a staircase, close the eye at high data rates and radiate EMI.
The fix is to match impedances and terminate: a series resistor at the source or a resistor at the load."
